Sri Lanka’s Ministry of Defense stated that Prabhakaran was among 19 high-ranking LTTE figures identified among the casualties recovered as troops completed final clearing operations following the routing of the Tigers. According to the ministry, these leaders included Prabhakaran’s eldest son, Charles Anthony, as well as Pottu Amman, the LTTE’s chief of intelligence.

Prabhakaran founded the militant organization, which has been designated a terrorist group by 32 nations. According to the FBI, the LTTE pioneered the deployment of female suicide bombers and invented the explosive suicide belt. It also holds the distinction of being the only terrorist organization to have successfully assassinated two world leaders. 

Prabhakaran was accused of masterminding the 1991 assassination of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi during an election campaign in the Tamil-dominated state of Tamil Nadu. Sri Lankan authorities maintain that Prabhakaran was retaliating against Gandhi’s decision to deploy Indian peacekeeping forces to Sri Lanka. Two years later, a Tiger suicide bomber—allegedly acting under Prabhakaran's direct orders—detonated an explosive device during a rally, killing Sri Lanka’s sitting president, Ranasinghe Premadasa.

Should the rebels honor this pledge, it would potentially signal the conclusion of Asia’s longest-running civil war.

To his supporters, Prabhakaran was viewed as a heroic figure with a single-minded devotion to fighting for the rights of his people. Conversely, the Sri Lankan government denounced him as a war criminal who operated with utter disregard for civilian casualties. He was wanted by Interpol on charges including terrorism and organized crime. Reports indicated that he routinely wore a cyanide capsule around his neck, prepared to take his own life rather than face capture—an unyielding standard of allegiance he demanded from his troops, which resulted in very few Tiger combatants ever being taken alive.

Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa is scheduled to address Parliament and the nation on Tuesday to formally announce the end of military operations against the Tiger rebels, amid ongoing concern from international aid agencies regarding the crisis. In response, representatives of the LTTE acknowledged the government's declaration of victory but did not immediately confirm Prabhakaran's death. Having founded the LTTE in the 1970s, Prabhakaran transformed the group into a highly disciplined combat force, ultimately leading to its designation as a terrorist organization by 32 nations. Under his command, the LTTE pioneered tactics that would redefine modern warfare and terrorism, most notably inventing the explosive suicide belt and routinely utilizing female suicide bombers to execute high-profile attacks.

Notably, it remains the only terrorist organization in history to have successfully assassinated two world leaders: former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, killed by a female suicide bomber in 1991, and former Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa, assassinated in a similar fashion in 1993.

***

# The End of Eelam War: The Fall of the LTTE and the Conclusion of the Sri Lankan Civil War

### Background: The Rise of a Violent Insurgency
For nearly three decades, the island nation of Sri Lanka was consumed by a devastating civil war. At the heart of the conflict was the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), a separatist militant organization founded in 1976 by Velupillai Prabhakaran. Seeking to establish an independent Tamil state—Tamil Eelam—in the north and east of the country, the LTTE grew from a small guerrilla band into one of the most sophisticated and ruthless insurgent forces in modern history. 

Unlike many rebel groups of its era, the LTTE developed conventional military capabilities, complete with a ground army, a naval wing (the Sea Tigers), and even a rudimentary air force (the Air Tigers). However, it was the group’s pioneer work in asymmetric warfare that drew global condemnation. The LTTE turned suicide terrorism into a organized doctrine through its elite wing, the Black Tigers. Credit with refining and popularizing the modern suicide belt and vest, the organization carried out hundreds of suicide attacks against military, economic, and civilian targets. 

The LTTE’s reach extended beyond national borders, demonstrating a capability to assassinate top-tier political figures. Among its high-profile targets were former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, who was assassinated by a female LTTE suicide bomber in 1991, and Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993. These high-profile political murders, combined with widespread extortion, forced recruitment (including of child soldiers), and ethnic cleansing, led to the LTTE being designated as a terrorist organization by dozens of countries, including the United States, India, Canada, and the member states of the European Union.

### The Turn toward Total War (2006–2008)
Following the collapse of a fragile 2002 Norwegian-mediated ceasefire, full-scale hostilities resumed in 2006. Under the leadership of President Mahinda Rajapaksa and Defense Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, the Sri Lankan government fundamentally shifted its strategy. Moving away from negotiated settlements, the administration resolved to entirely destroy the LTTE’s military capacity.

The Sri Lankan Armed Forces (SLAF) launched a massive, multi-front offensive. The Sri Lanka Navy systematically hunted and sank the LTTE's "floating warehouses"—merchant ships used to smuggle arms on the high seas—effectively cutting off the rebels' international resupply lines. Simultaneously, ground forces liberated the Eastern Province by mid-2007 before turning their full focus toward the LTTE’s heavily fortified northern strongholds in the Vanni region.

Despite fierce resistance and harsh terrain, the military’s numerical superiority, enhanced intelligence gathering, and heavy artillery support steadily compressed the territory held by the rebels. In January 2009, the government captured Kilinochchi, the administrative capital of the LTTE, forcing the remaining insurgent forces into a continuous retreat.

### The Final Battle and Mop-Up Operations (2009)
By early May 2009, the once-expansive Tamil Tiger territory had been reduced to a narrow, sandy strip of coastline around the Nanthikadal Lagoon near Mullaitivu. Trapped alongside the remaining insurgent fighters were tens of thousands of Tamil civilians, who were used by the LTTE as human shields in a desperate attempt to force an international intervention.

In the face of mounting international pressure regarding the high humanitarian cost and civilian casualties, the Sri Lankan military pressed forward with its final assault. Special forces and infantry units breached the LTTE's final defensive earthworks, isolating pockets of fighters and cutting off escape routes into the surrounding jungles and ocean.

The climax of the operation occurred between May 17 and May 19, 2009. Sri Lankan troops conducted intense mop-up operations around the Nanthikadal Lagoon to eliminate the last remnants of LTTE resistance. During these final encounters, the military wiped out the remaining senior leadership of the group. On the morning of May 19, 2009, the body of Velupillai Prabhakaran was discovered in the marshlands, alongside those of his top commanders, including intelligence chief Pottu Amman and Sea Tiger leader Soosai. 

### Aftermath and Legacy
On May 19, 2009, President Rajapaksa officially declared victory, ending a 26-year civil war that had claimed an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 lives. The total elimination of its core leadership, coupled with the capture of its final strongholds, resulted in the complete decimation of the LTTE.

The military victory was widely celebrated across Sri Lanka as the end of a long-standing terrorist threat, bringing a close to an era marked by constant fear of suicide bombings and political instability. Internationally, the collapse of the LTTE was studied by military strategists as a rare instance of a state achieving a complete military defeat over a powerful, deeply entrenched insurgent group.

However, the war's conclusion left a complex legacy. While the defeat of the LTTE ended decades of insurgent violence, the final months of the offensive drew intense international scrutiny regarding civilian casualties, allegations of war crimes, and the need for long-term political reconciliation between the ethnic Sinhalese majority and Tamil minority—challenges that Sri Lanka continues to navigate today.

**Colombo: The Pulsating Heart of Sri Lanka**

Nestled on the island’s sun-drenched southwestern coast, **Colombo** serves as the dynamic commercial capital and vibrant cultural gateway of **Sri Lanka**. It is a city of striking contrasts, where tropical warmth meets urban energy, and ancient heritage seamlessly weaves into a modern, fast-growing skyline. 

Stepping into **Colombo** is like walking through a living tapestry of history. Centuries of colonial influence—from the Portuguese and Dutch to the British—have left an indelible mark on the city's character. In the historic Fort district, restored colonial-era architecture stands proudly alongside sleek modern skyscrapers. The Dutch Hospital precinct, once a 17th-century medical facility, has transformed into a lively courtyard of high-end dining and boutique shopping. Just a short distance away, the futuristic Lotus Tower pierces the clouds, symbolizing **Sri Lanka’s** push toward the future.

The true soul of **Colombo**, however, lies in its rich cultural diversity and sensory experiences. The bustling neighborhood of Pettah offers a sensory sensory overload, where open-air markets overflow with aromatic spices, vibrant textiles, and shimmering jewelry. Amidst this energetic chaos stand remarkable places of worship, such as the candy-striped Jami Ul-Alfar Mosque (Red Mosque) and the tranquil Gangaramaya Temple, a Buddhist sanctuary sitting near the peaceful waters of Beira Lake.

As evening approaches, the city shifts its focus to the ocean. Locals and travelers alike gather at Galle Face Green, a sweeping seaside promenade that comes alive at sunset. Here, ocean breezes mix with the irresistible aromas of Sri Lankan street food—crispy *isso vadai* (prawn fritters), sizzling *kottu roti*, and fresh seafood prepared with aromatic local spices. Children fly kites, families stroll along the shore, and colorful tuk-tuks zip past against the backdrop of the glowing Indian Ocean.

While many travelers view **Colombo** merely as a transit stop on their way to the beaches or tea plantations of **Sri Lanka**, the city is a captivating destination in its own right. With its infectious energy, deep historical roots, and warm, welcoming spirit, **Colombo** perfectly captures the vibrant essence of modern **Sri Lanka**.

# Sri Lankan military: Tamil Tiger leader Velupillai Prabhakaran killed

**By CNN Staff**
**Updated 11:45 AM EDT, Monday, May 18, 2009**

**(CNN) —** Velupillai Prabhakaran, the founder and ruthless commander of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), has been killed by government forces in northern Sri Lanka, the country’s military announced Monday. 

The death of the elusive insurgent chief marks the decisive, blood-soaked end to a 26-year civil war that has claimed an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 lives and devastated the island nation.

Sri Lankan Army Commander Lt. Gen. Sarath Fonseka announced the news in a televised broadcast to the nation, stating that special forces had surrounded Prabhakaran in a small patch of jungle near the Nanthikadal lagoon, the insurgent group's final redoubt.

"We have successfully liberated the entire country from the clutches of terrorism," Fonseka said. "Today, we have defeated the terror group and killed its leader, Velupillai Prabhakaran."

According to senior defense officials, Prabhakaran was killed alongside his top lieutenants—including his intelligence chief, Pottu Amman, and naval commander, Soosai—while trying to break through advancing troops in an armored ambulance. State television later broadcast graphic footage showing what appeared to be Prabhakaran’s body, wearing a camouflage uniform with his trademark mustache and a gunshot wound to the forehead.

### LTTE Pushes Back Against Claims

The LTTE’s diplomatic chief, Selvarasa Pathmanathan, initially rejected the military's claims from an undisclosed location overseas, insisting that Prabhakaran was "alive and safe" and would continue to lead the fight for Tamil independence. 

However, reports from the frontline suggested the rebel leadership had completely collapsed. Just hours earlier, the LTTE’s official website had posted a statement admitting that the battle had reached its "bitter end" and announcing that the group had decided to "silence our guns."

### Architect of Modern Suicide Terrorism

For nearly three decades, the 54-year-old Prabhakaran commanded one of the world's most disciplined, brutal, and sophisticated insurgent organizations. 

Under his absolute command, the LTTE grew from a small guerrilla band in the late 1970s into a formidable military force complete with a standing army, a naval wing known as the Sea Tigers, and a rudimentary air force. The group sought an independent state—"Tamil Eelam"—for the island's Tamil minority, who complained of systemic discrimination by the Sinhalese majority.

Prabhakaran is widely credited with pioneering the modern use of the suicide belt. His elite suicide wing, the "Black Tigers," carried out hundreds of attacks against civilian, military, and political targets. 

Unlike many contemporary militant groups, Prabhakaran’s LTTE used suicide bombers not just as weapons of terror, but as precision military instruments. Among the group's most high-profile assassinations:

*   **1991:** The assassination of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi by a female suicide bomber in Tamil Nadu, India.
*   **1993:** The assassination of Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in a suicide bombing during a May Day rally in Colombo.

The group also targeted key economic infrastructure, including a devastating 1996 attack on the Central Bank in Colombo that killed 91 people, and a 2001 raid on the Sri Lankan international airport that destroyed half of the national airline's fleet. The LTTE was subsequently designated a terrorist organization by the United States, the European Union, India, and Canada.

### The War's Bloody Final Act

Prabhakaran's death follows a crushing three-year military offensive ordered by President Mahinda Rajapaksa, who abandoned a fragile 2002 Norwegian-brokered ceasefire to pursue a military solution to the conflict.

Driven out of their de facto state in the northern Vanni region, the Tigers were relentlessly pushed into a rapidly shrinking strip of coastline over the past several months. 

The final weeks of the conflict drew intense international concern. The United Nations and international human rights groups accused the Sri Lankan military of shelling heavy civilian zones and hospitals, while accusing the LTTE of using tens of thousands of trapped Tamil civilians as human shields and shooting those who attempted to flee.

### A Nation Celebrates, but Deep Fractures Remain

News of Prabhakaran’s death sparked spontaneous street parties in the capital city of Colombo, where crowds waved national flags, set off firecrackers, and danced in the streets to celebrate the end of a conflict that has defined Sri Lanka for a generation.

President Rajapaksa is expected to give a formal address to Parliament on Tuesday morning to officially declare total victory.

While the death of Prabhakaran effectively eliminates the LTTE as a conventional military force, political analysts warn that long-term peace is far from guaranteed. Sri Lanka now faces the monumental task of rebuilding a shattered north, resettling more than 250,000 displaced civilians currently held in government-run camps, and addressing the root political grievances of the Tamil minority that gave rise to Prabhakaran’s movement in the first place.

*CNN's staff in Colombo and Atlanta contributed to this report.*

### The Final Showdown

Addressing a jubilant Parliament, President Mahinda Rajapaksa formally announced the total military defeat of the rebels.

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon urged the Sri Lankan government to prioritize the immediate relief of hundreds of thousands of displaced Tamils held in military-run camps and called for an urgent political process to address the underlying causes of the ethnic conflict.

### The Road Ahead

With the LTTE’s military leadership wiped out, analysts note that Sri Lanka faces a daunting task in achieving lasting peace.

### SRI LANKA CIVIL WAR ENDS: LTTE Leader Velupillai Prabhakaran Killed, Military Says

Updated 11:45 AM EDT, Monday, May 18, 2009  
**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN)** — Velupillai Prabhakaran, the ruthless founder and leader of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), has been killed, Sri Lanka’s military announced Monday, effectively bringing an end to one of Asia’s longest and bloodiest civil wars.

* **26-Year War Ends:** Sri Lankan government declares total victory over the Tamil Tigers.

### A Violent End to a Decades-Long Rebellion

According to senior military officials, Prabhakaran was killed early Monday morning while trying to break out of the army's encirclement in a heavily armored ambulance near the Nanthikadal lagoon. 

"We have successfully liberated the entire country from terrorism," Lt. Gen. Fonseka said in a national address. "Today, we have annihilated the leadership of the LTTE."

Sri Lankan state television aired graphic footage showing the body of a man resembling Prabhakaran, dressed in camouflage attire, lying on a stretcher with a head wound. Military officials stated that DNA testing and physical identification by former rebel commanders confirmed his identity.

The death of the elusive warlord marks the cataclysmic collapse of the LTTE, a group that had waged a relentless 26-year campaign to create an independent Tamil state in the north and east of the island nation. 

### President Declares Total Victory

In Colombo, the capital, thousands of citizens flooded the streets, waving national flags, lighting firecrackers, and dancing to celebrate the news. 

Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa is expected to formally address Parliament on Tuesday to proclaim full control over the nation's territory for the first time since 1983. 

"The military task is complete," a spokesperson for the President’s office told CNN. "Our focus now turns to rebuilding the nation, restoring democracy to the north, and rehabilitating those who were displaced."

### The Shadow of the LTTE

For nearly three decades, Prabhakaran was the supreme leader of an organization renowned for its extreme discipline, tactical sophistication, and brutal violence. Under his command, the LTTE pioneered the use of suicide belts, establishing a specialized wing known as the "Black Tigers."

The group was designated a terrorist organization by more than 30 countries, including the United States, India, and the European Union. 

Prabhakaran was directly linked to high-profile assassinations, including former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 and Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993. At its peak, the LTTE operated a mini-state complete with its own army, navy, rudimentary air force, police, and taxation system.

### Humanitarian Toll and International Concern

While the Sri Lankan government celebrates a definitive military triumph, international human rights organizations and the United Nations have voiced grave concern over the conflict's human cost.

"The end of the fighting brings immense relief, but the humanitarian challenge ahead is staggering," a UN spokesperson said from Geneva. "Over 250,000 displaced Tamil civilians are currently housed in temporary camps, and an independent investigation into alleged war crimes by both sides is urgently needed."

### What Comes Next?

Analysts warn that while Prabhakaran’s death signals the end of the LTTE as a conventional military force, true peace will depend on how Sri Lanka addresses the root causes of Tamil political marginalization.

"Defeating the LTTE militarily is one thing," said Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu, director of the Colombo-based Centre for Policy Alternatives. "Winning the political peace and meaningfully integrating the minority Tamil population into the nation's political framework is the real challenge that begins today."
